newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian market blase about Japan oil product exports.
newsitem.headline: Asian market blase about Japan oil product exports.

text.p: Japan's decision to liberalise petroleum product exports may give its refiners more flexibility in getting goods to market but it is unlikely to lead to an inundation of Asian product markets, traders say.
"The news is certainly not bullish for Asian markets, but we aren't expecting any immediate negative impact on prices," said an oil products trader in Singapore.

Measures implemented by the Trade Ministry from Tuesday allow Japanese trading houses and oil companies the freedom to set export prices for their oil products, regardless of Japan's prevailing domestic market prices.
Previously, they were not allowed to set prices substantially different from domestic market levels -- which are typically much higher than other levels of other Asian markets.

And beginning July 14, oil product exporters will need to obtain government permission for exports only once a year, shipping their products overseas as many times as they like as long as their accumulated export volume is within a preset figure. Currently they need permission for each individual transaction.
"What the measure allows us to do is move more flexibly," said a trader with a Japanese refiner.
"We'll now be able to make smaller size exports whenever we want, which will naturally increase our export volumes," the trader added.
That freedom is a timely development for Japan's refining sector, which is currently suffering from a heavy surplus in inventories of middle-distillates.
Kerosene stocks stood 47.1 percent higher than a year earlier at end-May, while gas oil stocks were 9.6 percent higher.
But traders said market fears about Japan unloading significant volumes of excess product on Singapore spot markets were probably unrealistic as the material would likely be directed further north.

"The product destinations will still be northern China, South Korea, and Taiwan," said a trader with a Japanese refiner. One Singapore trader said that the relatively high prices fetched in Japan's domestic markets, as well as the higher quality of Japan's oil products, made shipments abroad a route of last resort.
"It will really be only a final option for them, as it will mean they will be selling a better product for less money," said the trader.

Most Japanese refiners are now producing gas oil with a 0.05 percent sulphur content, ahead of an October legislation which will require the cleaner burning specification for all material sold at the retail level.
Formerly the sulphur content was some four times higher, at 0.2 percent, the same level prevailing in Singapore spot markets.
Overall Japan product exports in May stood at 1.55 million kilolitres (314,000 barrels per day).
